claim: HIV-1 infection cannot be cured because the virus persists as integrated proviral DNA in long-lived cells despite years of suppressive antiretroviral therapy (ART).
source: HIV-1 infection cannot be cured because the virus persists as integrated proviral DNA in long-lived cells despite years of suppressive antiretroviral therapy (ART).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in HIV research, supported by extensive scientific literature and clinical observations.

claim: A median of 14% (range 0–42%) of the DNA sequences were defective due to G-to-A hypermutation.
source: A median of 14% (range 0–42%) of the DNA sequences were defective due to G-to-A hypermutation.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the study's sequencing data analysis.

claim: Remaining DNA sequences showed no evidence of evolution over years of suppressive ART.
source: Remaining DNA sequences showed no evidence of evolution over years of suppressive ART.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic and root-to-tip distance analyses of the sequencing data.

claim: Most sequences from the DNA reservoirs were very similar to viruses actively replicating in plasma (RNA sequences) shortly before start of ART.
source: Most sequences from the DNA reservoirs were very similar to viruses actively replicating in plasma (RNA sequences) shortly before start of ART.
evidence: This is based on comparative sequence analysis between pre-ART RNA and post-ART DNA samples.

claim: The results do not support persistent HIV-1 replication as a mechanism to maintain the HIV-1 reservoir during suppressive therapy.
source: The results do not support persistent HIV-1 replication as a mechanism to maintain the HIV-1 reservoir during suppressive therapy.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the lack of evolutionary changes in DNA sequences during ART.

claim: Suppressive ART halts the turnover of DNA variants.
source: Rather, the data indicate that DNA variants are turning over as long as patients are untreated and that suppressive ART halts this turnover.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DNA sequences match late pre-ART RNA sequences and show no evolution during ART.

claim: DNA variants are turning over as long as patients are untreated.
source: Rather, the data indicate that DNA variants are turning over as long as patients are untreated and that suppressive ART halts this turnover.
evidence: This is inferred from the overrepresentation of late pre-ART variants in the DNA reservoir.

claim: Combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) has had significant effects on the morbidity and mortality associated with human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection.
source: Combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) has had significant effects on the morbidity and mortality associated with human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the impact of ART on HIV outcomes.

claim: ART very effectively suppresses active virus replication.
source: ART very effectively suppresses active virus replication, but it cannot eradicate the infection because HIV-1 persists as integrated proviral DNA in long-lived cells that constitute a virus reservoir.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ART efficacy.

claim: ART cannot eradicate HIV-1 infection because HIV-1 persists as integrated proviral DNA in long-lived cells that constitute a virus reservoir.
source: ART very effectively suppresses active virus replication, but it cannot eradicate the infection because HIV-1 persists as integrated proviral DNA in long-lived cells that constitute a virus reservoir.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV persistence mechanisms.

claim: Latently infected resting memory CD4+ T-lymphocytes (memory CD4 cells) represent the most solidly documented HIV-1 reservoir.
source: Latently infected resting memory CD4+ T-lymphocytes (memory CD4 cells) represent the most solidly documented HIV-1 reservoir (Eriksson et al., 2013; Chun et al., 1997, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fully functional integrated HIV-1 proviruses are present in a small fraction of memory CD4 cells.
source: Fully functional integrated HIV-1 proviruses are present in a small fraction of memory CD4 cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV reservoir characteristics.

claim: Memory CD4 cells do not produce virus when they are in a resting state, but can be induced to produce virus upon activation in vitro and in vivo.
source: These cells do not produce virus when they are in a resting state, but can be induced to produce virus upon activation in vitro and in vivo (Eriksson et al., 2013; Chun et al., 1995, 1997; Massanella and Richman, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The activation state of the infected cell and the viral encoded Tat feedback loop jointly determine latency and virus production.
source: The activation state of the infected cell and the viral encoded Tat feedback loop jointly determine latency and virus production (Razooky et al., 2015; Rouzine et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The quantitative virus outgrowth assay (QVOA) has been the 'gold standard' for quantifying HIV-1 reservoirs.
source: The quantitative virus outgrowth assay (QVOA) has been the 'gold standard' (von Stockenstrom et al., 2015; Massanella and Richman, 2016; Bruner et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The QVOA greatly underestimates the true size of the functional reservoir.
source: but recent studies have revealed that this assay greatly underestimates the true size of the functional reservoir (Ho et al., 2013; Bruner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research findings.

claim: PCR-based assays overestimate the size of the functional reservoir because they cannot distinguish between replication-competent and defective viral genomes.
source: In contrast, PCR-based assays overestimate the size of the functional reservoir because they cannot distinguish between replication-competent and defective viral genomes (von Stockenstrom et al., 2015; Massanella and Richman, 2016; Bruner et al., 2015, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Many defective proviruses contain large internal deletions.
source: Many defective proviruses contain large internal deletions (Ho et al., 2013; Sanchez et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Defective proviruses result from APOBEC editing, which induces G-to-A hypermutation.
source: Defective proviruses also result from APOBEC editing, which induces G-to-A hypermutation (Yu et al., 2004; Kieffer et al., 2005; Stopak et al., 2003; Bruner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The HIV-1 reservoir is established early during primary infection.
source: The HIV-1 reservoir is established early during primary infection and is remarkably quantitatively and qualitatively stable.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV reservoir dynamics.

claim: The HIV-1 reservoir is remarkably quantitatively and qualitatively stable.
source: The HIV-1 reservoir is established early during primary infection and is remarkably quantitatively and qualitatively stable.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV reservoir dynamics.

claim: Siliciano et al. (2003) found a 44-month half-life for latently infected cells capable of producing replication-competent virus in the QVOA.
source: Siliciano et al. (2003) found a 44-month half-life for latently infected cells capable of producing replication-competent virus in the QVOA.
evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited study.

claim: HIV-1 DNA levels and genetic compositions are very stable in patients receiving long-term suppressive ART.
source: Similarly, HIV-1 DNA levels and genetic compositions are very stable in patients receiving long-term suppressive ART (von Stockenstrom et al., 2015; Besson et al., 2014; Josefsson et al., 2013; Kearney et al., 2014; Günthard et al., 1999; Evering et al., 2012; Kieffer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Early ART reduces the reservoir's size and genetic complexity.
source: Early ART reduces the reservoir's size and genetic complexity (Chomont et al., 2009; Josefsson et al., 2013; Lori et al., 1999; Strain et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Most studies suggest that the HIV-1 reservoir is maintained by the physiological homeostasis of memory CD4 cells that in part involves occasional expansion and contraction of individual CD4 cell clones.
source: Most studies suggest that the HIV-1 reservoir is maintained by the physiological homeostasis of memory CD4 cells that in part involves occasional expansion and contraction of individual CD4 cell clones (von Stockenstrom et al., 2015; Chomont et al., 2011, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some studies have suggested that persistent virus replication may be an important contributor to the maintenance of the HIV-1 reservoir.
source: However, the results of some studies have suggested that persistent virus replication may be an important contributor to the maintenance of the HIV-1 reservoir (Buzón et al., 2010; Yukl et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Lorenzo-Redondo et al. (2016) reported evidence of rapid HIV-1 evolution in lymphoid tissue reservoirs.
source: Recently, Lorenzo-Redondo et al. (2016) reported evidence of rapid HIV-1 evolution in lymphoid tissue reservoirs.
evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited study.

claim: The study population consisted of 10 HIV-1 infected patients who were diagnosed in Sweden between 1990 and 2003.
source: The study population consisted of 10 HIV-1 infected patients who were diagnosed in Sweden between 1990 and 2003.
evidence: This describes the study cohort.

claim: The HIV-1 DNA sequences recapitulate the diversity observed in RNA sequences before treatment, often with exact sequence matches.
source: The HIV-1 DNA sequences recapitulate the diversity observed in RNA sequences before treatment, often with exact sequence matches, Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is based on comparative sequence analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Haplotype abundance varied between 0.1 and 50% in sequence read frequencies.
source: While we observed large variations in the abundance of haplotypes with sequence read frequencies varying between 0.1 and 50% (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the sequencing data.

claim: Variation in haplotype abundance likely reflects clonal expansion, independent integration of identical sequences, and resampling of the same original DNA templates during sequencing.
source: Variation in haplotype abundance likely reflects clonal expansion (Josefsson et al., 2013; von Stockenstrom et al., 2015), independent integration of identical sequences, and resampling of the same original DNA templates during sequencing.
evidence: This is an inference about the causes of observed variation, supported by citations.

claim: Substantial proportions (median 14%; range 0–42%) of the p17gag DNA sequences from the viral reservoirs were hypermutated and were therefore expected to be replication incompetent.
source: We found that substantial proportions (median 14%; range 0–42%) of the p17gag DNA sequences from the viral reservoirs were hypermutated and were therefore expected to be replication incompetent (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the sequencing data analysis.

claim: This result was consistent with the results of earlier research, which showed that 9–30% of sequences were hypermutated.
source: This result was consistent with the results of earlier research, which showed that 9–30% of sequences were hypermutated (Josefsson et al., 2013; Bruner et al., 2015; Kieffer et al., 2005).
evidence: This compares the current findings to previous studies.

claim: A small proportion of sequences had stop codons that were not obviously due to G-to-A hypermutation (mean 3%, range 0–12%).
source: A small proportion of sequences had stop codons that were not obviously due to G-to-A hypermutation (mean 3%, range 0–12%).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the sequencing data analysis.

claim: A proportion of sequences without overt inactivating mutations were likely also replication incompetent due to mutations or deletions outside of p17gag.
source: A proportion of sequences without overt inactivating mutations were likely also replication incompetent due to mutations or deletions outside of p17gag (Ho et al., 2013; Bruner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge from cited studies.

claim: Plasma HIV-1 RNA populations obtained before the start of ART evolved at a relatively constant rate.
source: Plasma HIV-1 RNA populations obtained before the start of ART evolved at a relatively constant rate (Zanini et al., 2015); there was a steady increase in mean root-to-tip distances over time in Figure 3.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in the figure and cited previous work.

claim: The HIV-1 DNA populations obtained after 3–18 years of suppressive therapy had stable root-to-tip distances.
source: In sharp contrast, the HIV-1 DNA populations obtained after 3–18 years of suppressive therapy had stable root-to-tip distances.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of the sequencing data.

claim: Hypermutated DNA sequences had larger root-to-tip distances, but these distances were also stable over time.
source: Hypermutated DNA sequences had larger root-to-tip distances, but these distances were also stable over time (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: In all 10 patients, statistically significant evolution of plasma RNA sequences was found before the start of therapy, with rates 1−4 × 10−3/year.
source: In all 10 patients we found statistically significant evolution of plasma RNA sequences before the start of therapy, with rates 1−4 × 10−3/year.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the sequencing data.

claim: DNA sequences showed no signal of statistically significant evolution in DNA reservoirs during suppressive ART.
source: In contrast, DNA sequences showed no signal of statistically significant evolution in DNA reservoirs during suppressive ART.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the sequencing data.

claim: Approximately 60% of the DNA reads were most similar to RNA variants that were present in plasma samples obtained during the last year before the start of therapy.
source: A combined analysis of the data for all patients (Figure 4, panel C) indicated that approximately 60% of the DNA reads were most similar to RNA variants that were present in plasma samples obtained during the last year before the start of therapy.
evidence: This is based on comparative sequence analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The representation of the variants present in the earlier plasma samples decreased with a half-life of 0.75 years going backward in time from the start of therapy.
source: The representation of the variants present in the earlier plasma samples decreased; the half-life was 0.75 years going backward in time from the start of therapy.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of the sequence data.

claim: On average approximately 5% of the reads matched plasma variants from the first 6 months after the estimated date of infection (EDI).
source: On average approximately 5% of the reads matched plasma variants from the first 6 months after the estimated date of infection (EDI) (Figure 4, panel B).
evidence: This is based on comparative sequence analysis shown in the figure.

claim: If the outlying data for patient six were omitted, the fraction of reads matching early variants was 2%.
source: If the outlying data for patient six were omitted, this fraction was 2%.
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of the data excluding one patient.

claim: If the rates of seeding into the reservoirs were stable over time, we would have expected a mean value of 0.14% (range < 0.001–0.32% across patients) of the DNA sequences to match the earliest plasma variants.
source: If the rates of seeding into the reservoirs were stable over time, we would have expected a mean value of 0.14% (range < 0.001–0.32% across patients) of the DNA sequences to match the earliest plasma variants.
evidence: This is a theoretical calculation based on assumptions about seeding rates.

claim: Massive seeding of HIV DNA into the viral reservoirs occurred during the first weeks and months post-infection.
source: This result suggested that massive seeding of HIV DNA into the viral reservoirs occurred during the first weeks and months post-infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the overrepresentation of early variants compared to expected values.

claim: Viral variants that replicated shortly before the start of suppressive ART were overrepresented in the HIV-1 DNA reservoirs.
source: In summary, viral variants that replicated shortly before the start of suppressive ART were overrepresented in the HIV-1 DNA reservoirs.
evidence: This is based on comparative sequence analysis.

claim: The infected cells were turning over with approximately one-year half-life for as long as the patients were untreated.
source: This result indicated that the infected cells were turning over (approximately one-year half-life) for as long as the patients were untreated.
evidence: This is inferred from the decay rate of earlier variants in the reservoir.

claim: The reservoir HIV-1 DNA populations were remarkably stable and showed no evidence of active replication during ART.
source: The reservoir HIV-1 DNA populations were remarkably stable and showed no evidence of active replication during ART.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic and evolutionary rate analyses.

claim: Sequences in HIV-1 DNA reservoirs mainly derived from the populations present during the last year before the start of suppressive therapy.
source: In particular, we were able to show that sequences in HIV-1 DNA reservoirs mainly derived from the populations present during the last year before the start of suppressive therapy.
evidence: This is based on comparative sequence analysis.

claim: Lorenzo-Redondo et al. (2016) reported very high rates of evolution (7.4−12 × 10−3 changes per site per year), which are approximately 3- to 5-fold greater than those typically observed in gag and pol of replicating RNA populations.
source: The authors reported very high rates of evolution (7.4−12 × 10−3 changes per site per year); these rates are approximately 3- to 5-fold greater than those typically observed in gag and pol of replicating RNA populations.
evidence: This is a comparison of reported rates from a cited study to typical rates.

claim: Such rapid evolution is incompatible with the lack of observable changes in the reservoir sequences over the 20 times longer time intervals reported in this study.
source: Such rapid evolution is incompatible with the lack of observable changes in the reservoir sequences over the 20 times longer time intervals reported here (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference comparing the current findings to those of Lorenzo-Redondo et al.

claim: It is possible that the reported temporal signal by Lorenzo-Redondo et al. arises from changes in DNA reservoir composition during the first 6 months of therapy when short-lived cells infected with recently replicating virus variants gradually disappear.
source: It is possible that the reported temporal signal arises from changes in DNA reservoir composition during the first 6 months of therapy when short-lived cells infected with recently replicating virus variants gradually disappear.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the findings of Lorenzo-Redondo et al.

claim: Death of short-lived cells increases the proportions of longer-lived cells that sample further back into the history of the infection.
source: Death of short-lived cells increases the proportions of longer-lived cells that sample further back into the history of the infection.
evidence: This is an inference about cell population dynamics.

claim: Changes in cell populations can create an impression of 'backward' evolution towards older HIV variants due the preferential pruning of later variants.
source: Instead these changes can create an impression of 'backward' evolution towards older HIV variants due the preferential pruning of later variants.
evidence: This is an inference about how sampling bias could affect evolutionary analyses.

claim: Lorenzo-Redondo et al. found similar rates in PBMC compared to tissue samples.
source: However, Lorenzo-Redondo et al. found similar rates in PBMC compared to tissue samples.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a cited study.

claim: Tissue and blood HIV-1 DNA variants should be well-mixed during the time period investigated.
source: Furthermore, tissue and blood HIV-1 DNA variants should be well-mixed during the time period that we investigated (Josefsson et al., 2013; von Stockenstrom et al., 2015; Lorenzo-Redondo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The absence of provirus evolution or turnover does not fully exclude the possibility that there was replication and evolution of replication-competent viruses present in the reservoirs.
source: The absence of provirus evolution or turnover does not fully exclude the possibility that there was replication and evolution of replication-competent viruses present in the reservoirs.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study's conclusions.

claim: If replication of replication-competent viruses occurred, it involved a minority of infected cells and occurred below the detection limit of the deep-sequencing method.
source: However, if such replication occurred, it involved a minority of infected cells and occurred below the detection limit of the deep-sequencing method.
evidence: This is an inference about the limits of detection in the study.

claim: The finding of genetic stability in the DNA reservoirs is consistent with Josefsson et al. (2013) and von Stockenstrom et al. (2015).
source: Our finding of genetic stability in the DNA reservoirs is consistent with Josefsson et al. (2013) and von Stockenstrom et al. (2015).
evidence: This compares the current findings to previous studies.

claim: Josefsson et al. and von Stockenstrom et al. found that defective HIV-1 DNA integrants present during long-term effective ART appear to be maintained by proliferation and longevity of infected cells and not by ongoing viral replication.
source: They found that defective HIV-1 DNA integrants present during long-term effective ART appear to be maintained by proliferation and longevity of infected cells and not by ongoing viral replication.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from cited studies.

claim: A majority of the variants present in the HIV-1 DNA reservoirs were derived from HIV-1 RNA variants that had replicated during the last year before the start of suppressive ART.
source: We found that a majority of the variants present in the HIV-1 DNA reservoirs were derived from HIV-1 RNA variants that had replicated during the last year before the start of suppressive ART.
evidence: This is based on comparative sequence analysis.

claim: Frenkel et al. (2003) reported the persistence of greater numbers of earlier versus more recent virus variants in a few children receiving suppressive ART.
source: In contrast, Frenkel et al. (2003) reported the persistence of greater numbers of earlier versus more recent virus variants in a few children receiving suppressive ART.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a cited study.

claim: Early variants were overrepresented relative to the expected level if deposition had been uniform over time.
source: These early variants were overrepresented relative to the expected level if deposition had been uniform over time.
evidence: This is based on comparison of observed to expected frequencies.

claim: The overrepresentation of early variants could be due to the high viral load present during primary HIV-1 infection.
source: This overrepresentation could be due to the high viral load present during primary HIV-1 infection and is consistent with results by Bruner et al. (2016), who found that defective proviruses rapidly accumulate during acute HIV-1 infection.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Bruner et al. (2016) found that defective proviruses rapidly accumulate during acute HIV-1 infection.
source: This overrepresentation could be due to the high viral load present during primary HIV-1 infection and is consistent with results by Bruner et al. (2016), who found that defective proviruses rapidly accumulate during acute HIV-1 infection.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a cited study.

claim: An excess of early variants was observed in only 5 out 10 patients.
source: However, we observed such an excess of early variants in only 5 out 10 patients.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data analysis.

claim: Defective HIV-1 proviruses are unique in vivo labels of individual memory CD4 cell clones.
source: Defective HIV-1 proviruses are unique in vivo labels of individual memory CD4 cell clones.
evidence: This is an inference about the utility of defective proviruses as markers.

claim: Defective proviruses can be used to track the fates of the memory CD4 cells, similar to the sequencing of T-cell receptors.
source: Similar to the sequencing of T-cell receptors, these labels can be used to track the fates of the memory CD4 cells (Robins, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Imamichi et al. (2014) found that a T-cell clone carrying a defective HIV-1 provirus can persist for >17 years.
source: This strategy was used by Imamichi et al. (2014), who found that a T-cell clone carrying a defective HIV-1 provirus can persist for >17 years.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a cited study.

claim: Prenatally formed T-cell receptors shared by twins have lifetimes that are >30 years.
source: Similarly, prenatally formed T-cell receptors shared by twins have lifetimes that are >30 years (Pogorelyy et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a cited study.

claim: The results are consistent with long T-cell life times once HIV replication is suppressed by ART.
source: Our results are consistent with such long T-cell life times once HIV replication is suppressed by ART.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the current findings to previous studies.

claim: In untreated infection, infected cells turn over with a half-life of approximately one year.
source: In untreated infection, however, we estimate much faster turnover of infected cells with a half-life of approximately one year.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the decay of earlier variants in the reservoir.

claim: Earlier studies based on different types of CD4 cell labelling have indicated that CD4 cell die at a 3- to 4-fold increased rate in untreated HIV-1-infected patients, compared with uninfected individuals and with patients receiving suppressive ART.
source: The results of earlier studies, which were based on different types of CD4 cell labelling, have indicated that CD4 cell die at a 3- to 4-fold increased rate in untreated HIV-1-infected patients, compared with uninfected individuals and with patients receiving suppressive ART (Hellerstein et al., 1999; McCune et al., 2000; Ribeiro et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about findings from cited studies.

claim: The more dramatic difference observed in this study might be due to that earlier studies estimated lifespans of individual cells, whereas this study estimated the lifespans of CD4 cell clones carrying defective proviruses.
source: The more dramatic difference that we observed might be due to that earlier studies estimated lifespans of individual cells, whereas we estimated the lifespans of CD4 cell clones carrying defective proviruses (i.e., infected cells and their daughter cells).
evidence: This is an inference about why the current findings differ from previous studies.

claim: The study did not sort cells and therefore could not investigate whether there were differences in HIV-1 turnover rates between different types and subsets of cells.
source: We did not sort cells and therefore could not investigate whether there were differences in HIV-1 turnover rates between different types and subsets of cells (e.g., memory CD4 cells and their subsets).
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study design.

claim: It is reasonable to assume that most of the HIV-1 DNA sequences were from memory CD4+ T-lymphocytes because others have found that these cells are the main HIV-1 reservoir.
source: However, it is reasonable to assume that most of our HIV-1 DNA sequences were from memory CD4+ T-lymphocytes because others have found that these cells are the main HIV-1 reservoir (Eriksson et al., 2013; Chun et al., 1997, 1995).
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge from cited studies.

claim: Because the study sequenced a relatively short region of the HIV-1 genome, it could not reliably distinguish between replication-competent and defective viruses.
source: Because we sequenced a relatively short region of the HIV-1 genome, we could not reliably distinguish between replication-competent and defective viruses.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study design.

claim: The study cannot rule out the possibility that a small subset of viruses was replicating and remained undetected among the many defective viruses.
source: We did not find evidence of evolution in proviral DNA sequences, but we cannot rule out the possibility that a small subset of viruses was replicating and remained undetected among the many defective viruses.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study's conclusions.

claim: The analyses of the composition and turnover of the virus reservoir were aided by the fact that most of the viruses were defective because these proviruses acted as inert in vivo labels of CD4 cell clones.
source: However, our analyses of the composition and turnover of the virus reservoir were aided by the fact that most of the viruses were defective because these proviruses acted as inert in vivo labels of CD4 cell clones.
evidence: This is an inference about how defective proviruses facilitated the analysis.

claim: Large variations in the abundance of sequence haplotypes likely indicate the presence of clonal expansions, independent integrations of identical sequences, and resampling of the same original DNA templates during sequencing.
source: We observed large variations in the abundance of sequence haplotypes that likely indicate the presence of clonal expansions (Josefsson et al., 2013; von Stockenstrom et al., 2015), independent integrations of identical sequences, and resampling of the same original DNA templates during sequencing.
evidence: This is an inference about the causes of observed variation, supported by citations.

claim: Given the sequencing method, the relative contributions of clonal expansion, independent integration, and PCR resampling mechanisms could not be determined.
source: Given our sequencing method, we could not determine the relative contributions of these mechanisms.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study design.

claim: The study is using Primer ID sequencing to better understand the in vivo dynamics of different viral haplotypes.
source: We are using Primer ID sequencing (Jabara et al., 2011) to better understand the in vivo dynamics of different viral haplotypes.
evidence: This describes ongoing work to address study limitations.

claim: Analysis of HIV integration sites represents an alternative method of clonal expansion identification.
source: Analysis of HIV integration sites represents an alternative method of clonal expansion identification (Maldarelli et al., 2014; Cohn et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Integration site analysis was not possible because the study did not sequence the extreme ends of the LTRs.
source: However, such analysis was not possible for us because we did not sequence the extreme ends of the LTRs.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study design.

claim: The study analyzed p17gag because it was part of the plasma HIV RNA dataset and because it has sufficient genetic diversity to allow for accurate and valid comparisons between plasma RNA and PBMC DNA HIV populations.
source: We analyzed p17gag because it was part of our plasma HIV RNA dataset and because it has sufficient genetic diversity to allow for accurate and valid comparisons between plasma RNA and PBMC DNA HIV populations.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the choice of genomic region.

claim: Results from several analyses suggested that clonal expansion did not affect the results in a qualitative manner.
source: Results from several analyses suggested that clonal expansion did not affect our results in a qualitative manner.
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analyses of the data.

claim: Cohn et al. (2015) found only a limited decrease in single integrations following the start of ART (from approximately 70 to 50%).
source: Consistent with our results and interpretation, Cohn et al. (2015) found only a limited decrease in single integrations following the start of ART (from approximately 70 to 50%).
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a cited study.

claim: T-cell turnover slowed down dramatically when ART began.
source: We also found that most of the latently infected cells present during long-term suppressive ART were infected shortly before the start of ART, and that T-cell turnover slowed down dramatically when ART began.
evidence: This is inferred from the stability of DNA sequences and the overrepresentation of late pre-ART variants.
